item.title: Burn the fleet, keep the semicolon
item.description: A civilisation rarely declines because it forgets how to build ships. It declines because it decides that building ships is not the sort of thing serious people do.
item.content:encoded:
In 1405 a Chinese fleet left Nanjing that no other power on earth could have assembled. Zheng He’s ships made seven voyages over 28 years, reaching Hormuz and the Swahili coast half a century before a Portuguese caravel managed the same water going the other way. Then it stopped. Within a few years of the Xuande emperor’s death in 1435 the civil bureaucracy had dissolved the naval offices, broken up the seagoing vessels and closed the routes.

The comfortable version blames hidebound Confucian xenophobes. The better version, argued by Yiu Siu in the Journal of Chinese History, will be wearily familiar to anyone who has sat on a budget committee. The emperor had built the fleet as an off-books enterprise: the tax system paid for it, the palace kept the trade profits. The mandarinate was funding a business it could never book revenue from. So when a child emperor came to the throne and their moment arrived, the bureaucrats did not merely stop the voyages. They built a fiscal firewall to stop any future emperor trying it again.

The most capable maritime organisation on earth was dismantled by intelligent people optimising correctly inside a badly drawn set of incentives. Nobody in the room was stupid. That is the whole problem.

15th Century Gateway Review

Any system that rewards conformity to inherited form over judgement about substance will eventually be overtaken by one that does not — because only the second kind can notice when the map has stopped matching the territory. The first kind has hired, promoted and ennobled people specifically for their fluency with the map. Asking them to look up is asking them to write down their own assets.

You see the junior version of this every week. The Bluebook is a citation system with a priesthood, a schism and a new edition every few years for reasons no practising lawyer has satisfactorily explained. Methodology has become a status word — a section you write to prove you are the sort of person who writes one. None of it began as vanity: citation formats exist so a reader can find the source, house style so a document can be read quickly by someone who did not draft it. The failure is the substitution. At some point the apparatus stopped asking does this work and started asking is this correct, and only the second question comes with a marking rubric.

So the semicolon gets policed and the clause that quietly reallocates the risk does not. Nobody in recorded history has been harmed by a comma splice. People are ruined every day by contracts drafted immaculately in the wrong direction.

Why heirs are a macroeconomic problem

Intelligence is substantially heritable. It is not transmissible. Galton worked out the difference in 1886 and gave us the phrase: regression to the mean. Clever parents have clever children, but on average less so. It is arithmetic, not ideology, and it is the single most reliably ignored fact in the history of elites.

Now add the behaviour of every parent who ever loved a child. Advantage passes down whole while ability regresses, and the gap between the position inherited and the ability inherited has to be filled with something. What fills it is form: the right school, the right register, the right way of holding a fork at the right sort of lunch. Credentialism is not a symptom of a stratified society. It is the load-bearing structure — the mechanism by which a mediocre heir is made legible as a superior person.

The cost is not moral, it is measured in output. Hsieh, Hurst, Jones and Klenow estimated in Econometrica that between a fifth and two-fifths of the growth in American output per person from 1960 to 2010 came from nothing more exotic than letting women and black men into the professions. Not from inventing anything. From no longer excluding people who were already there. Running the same logic forward, Bell, Chetty and colleagues found children of top-1% families are about ten times likelier to become inventors than children from below-median families — and the gap persists between children with the same early-childhood maths scores. The talent was measured. It was present. It simply was not in the room where inventing happens.

A society that hands positions to heirs is not being unfair in some abstract way that need trouble nobody. It is choosing to run at three-fifths capacity, and then wondering aloud why the other lot are building the ships.

A worked example

Which brings us, with a certain grim inevitability, to Donald Trump — interesting not as a villain but as a specimen. Villains are rare and usually competent. He is the purest available demonstration of what happens when a society’s machinery for identifying merit has been replaced by machinery for laundering inheritance.

A New York Times investigation in 2018, built on over a hundred thousand pages of records, found he received the equivalent of at least $413m from his father. His companies then filed for bankruptcy six times. Enterprise involves failure and there is no shame in a collapsed venture, but there is something very special about going bankrupt while running a casino. The house is meant to win. That is not a strategy, it is the architecture of the building.

He has said for decades that he graduated first in his class at Wharton. The dean’s list for his cohort is public. It is 56 names long. He is not on it, nor among the honours recipients in the 1968 commencement programme. He is simply an insecure liar who did not attend the top of his class and has spent sixty years citing it. In 2016 he paid $25m to settle fraud claims over Trump University. In 2024 a New York court found he had inflated asset values for years; an appellate panel threw out the penalty as unconstitutionally excessive in August 2025, but the fraud finding stood. And on 2 January 2021, recorded, he asked Georgia’s secretary of state for a number: “I just want to find 11,780 votes.”

Not count. Find.

A man who believes he actually won asks for a recount. Requesting a specific quantity is the behaviour of someone who has spent a lifetime discovering that the form can be made to say whatever is required, because nobody in his world was ever checking the substance. It worked on lenders. It worked on licensees. It worked on television. It worked on voters. Why would it not work on a state?

Why this style of leadership always loses in the end

In a few years it will be remarkably difficult to find anyone who admits to having supported Trump and his cronies.

This is not a prediction, it is a pattern with a very good record. In 1945 France discovered it had been, almost to a man, a nation of resisters — a retrospective unanimity so complete that Henry Rousso eventually had to coin a word for it, résistancialisme. The Communist Party styled itself the party of the 75,000 martyrs; the real figure was likely a few thousand. In occupied Germany, former party members obtained testimonials of clean political conduct from neighbours and victims, and the Germans, who are good at naming things, called them Persilscheine — Persil certificates, after the laundry detergent. Washed clean. Eight and a half million people had joined the Nazi Party. By 1949 you could not find them.

And this is where the argument closes on itself, because the disappearance is not merely hypocrisy. It is a measurement failure of exactly the kind that burned the fleet.

A leader who demands loyalty can only ever grade its form: the salute, the applause, the sufficiently enthusiastic public statement. He cannot measure the substance, because the one honest signal — someone willing to tell him he is wrong — is the first thing his system selects out. So he counts salutes and books them as a constituency. The numbers look magnificent right up to the morning they turn out to have been denominated in a currency nobody was actually holding. Ask Mr. Putin about his Ukrainian intelligence briefings.

Nor is the man at the top placed to notice. The figurehead is rarely the author of these arrangements; he is what they select for — the sociopath with enough nerve to take the job and not enough sense to see where it ends. He believes the salutes because nothing in his life has ever obliged him to check one, and checking is precisely the faculty the apparatus was built to filter out.

That is why these regimes do not decline gracefully. They are load-bearing right until they are vapour. The apparatus that grades form cannot see its own collapse coming, because collapse is a fact about substance and it stopped collecting that data years ago.

The Ming had the ships. Britain, before Crimea shamed it into competitive examination, had the officers. America has the best-trained professional workforce ever assembled. In none of these cases was the defect capability. The defect was governance — the slow, reasonable, minuted decision to reward fidelity to a form over judgement about a substance, until nobody in the building was being paid to notice that the map had come loose from the territory.

The fleets do not burn because somebody hates ships. They burn because the meeting ran to schedule, the paperwork was in order, and the item was carried.
